analysis.one_liner: Permanently repeals the federal estate tax and locks in low gift tax rates.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 37 Republican Senate cosponsors, the bill was referred to the Finance Committee, never received a vote, and died when the 112th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would permanently repeal the federal estate tax and the generation-skipping transfer tax, which are levied when very large estates pass to heirs. It would also permanently set the top gift tax rate at 35% with a $5 million lifetime exemption, letting wealthy families give away up to $5 million tax-free. Because the estate tax only applies to estates above roughly $5 million per person (about $10 million per couple), repeal would benefit a small group of the largest inheritances and reduce federal revenue.
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs to the largest estates — those above the roughly $5 million-per-person exemption — along with wealthy families who want to pass on or give away large sums without federal tax. The IRS reports the tax touches only a small fraction of all estates; most families never owe it.
analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury, and ultimately other taxpayers, would bear the lost revenue. Estate tax receipts would disappear while government spending continues, so the cost is made up through other taxes, less spending, or borrowing. Everyone who pays federal taxes shares that cost; the direct beneficiaries of repeal are concentrated at the top.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers generally, via lost revenue
analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits flow almost entirely to the wealthiest households, since the estate tax already exempts most estates and only applies to the largest inheritances. Its cost is broad but diffuse: lost federal revenue made up by other taxpayers or borrowing. Supporters argue the tax forces families to sell farms and businesses to pay the bill and amounts to double taxation of savings; the counter is that the exemption level already shields most small farms and businesses, and the law allows payment deferral for closely held businesses. The core design question is whether a tax on the very largest inheritances is worth the revenue it raises.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in the Senate and sent to the Finance Committee, which never took it up; it died there when the Congress ended.
outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The federal Treasury kept the estate tax revenue, and the tax remained on the books for large estates. Supporters of repeal gained nothing; the bill's only effect was that permanent repeal never advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The Treasury, which kept the estate tax

for.name: John Thune
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited a bloc of Republican cosponsors.

for.name: 37 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the estate tax repeal bill.

against.name: Max Baucus
against.what_they_did: The bill was referred to the Finance Committee, which took no action on it — no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: All 37 cosponsors were Republicans and the sponsor was Republican; no Democrat signed on, and the Democratic-run Senate committee never moved the bill.

industries.note: Repeal would eliminate the federal tax on estates above roughly $5 million per person, sparing the largest inheritances entirely. The revenue is a small but real share of federal receipts, so the lost cost falls on everyone else through other taxes or borrowing.

industries.industry: Estate planning and trust services (lawyers, wealth advisors)
industries.note: Much of this industry's business is structuring estates to reduce or avoid estate tax; repeal would remove the tax and much of the need for that planning. In this bill, their interest in keeping the tax runs alongside the public's interest in the revenue it raises.
